questions.prompt: What does 'Number of Threads (users)' set in a Thread Group?
options: How many virtual users run the group's samplers in parallel
How many requests per second are sent
How many CPU threads JMeter may use
How many times each sampler repeats
questions.explanation: It is the number of concurrent virtual users. Requests per second depend on response and think times, CPU threads are not configurable here, and repetition is the loop count.

questions.prompt: With 60 threads and a ramp-up period of 120 seconds, when does the last thread start (approximately)?
options: After about 118 seconds (one new thread every 2 seconds)
Immediately
After 60 seconds
After 7,200 seconds
questions.explanation: Ramp-up spreads starts evenly: 120 / 60 = one thread every 2 s, so the 60th starts near the end of the 120 s ramp-up.

questions.prompt: Ticking 'Infinite' for loop count without a duration makes the Thread Group run until you stop it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Infinite loops never end on their own; use Specify thread lifetime (duration) or stop manually.

questions.prompt: A test uses 100 threads, ramp-up 10 s, loop count 1. Each journey takes 30 s. What is the problem with this workload?
options: Threads finish after one journey, so the test never holds a steady state of 100 users for long
Ramp-up must be at least equal to the thread count in seconds
Loop count 1 is invalid
100 threads cannot start in 10 seconds
questions.explanation: With one loop each user leaves after about 30 s, so load peaks briefly and falls. For a steady state use more loops or a duration. There is no rule linking ramp-up to thread count, and starting 10 threads/s is fine.

questions.prompt: What does 'Same user on each iteration' (ticked by default) control?
options: Whether cookies and cache are kept between iterations of a thread, as if the same user continued
Whether every thread logs in as the same account
Whether iterations run in the same order
Whether the thread uses the same CSV row each time
questions.explanation: When unticked, JMeter clears cookie and cache managers at each iteration to simulate a new user. It does not pick accounts or CSV rows.

questions.prompt: Which statements about setUp and tearDown Thread Groups are correct? Select all that apply.
options: setUp runs before the regular Thread Groups
tearDown runs after the regular Thread Groups finish
They are a good place to create and delete test data
Variables set in setUp are automatically visible in the other Thread Groups
questions.explanation: setUp and tearDown frame the test and suit data preparation and cleanup. Variables are per thread, so to pass a value across groups you must use a property (for example props.put or __setProperty).

questions.prompt: You need to keep 50 users active for 20 minutes after a 5-minute ramp-up. Which configuration fits?
options: Threads 50, ramp-up 300 s, loop Infinite, 'Specify thread lifetime' with duration 1500 s
Threads 50, ramp-up 300 s, loop 20
Threads 1000, ramp-up 1200 s, loop 1
Threads 50, ramp-up 0, duration 1200 s
questions.explanation: The duration includes the ramp-up, so 300 + 1200 = 1500 s. A loop count of 20 gives an unknown duration, 1,000 threads is a different workload, and zero ramp-up spikes all users at once while 1200 s misses the 5-minute ramp.

questions.prompt: A Thread Group is set to 20 threads, ramp-up 60 s, duration 30 s. Testers notice only about 10 users ever ran. Why?
options: The duration ended the test after 30 s, halfway through the ramp-up, so the remaining threads never started
JMeter caps ramp-up at 30 s
Threads start in pairs
The loop count defaults to 0
questions.explanation: Duration is wall-clock from the start; at 1 thread every 3 s only about 10 threads start before 30 s. There is no ramp-up cap, threads start one at a time, and the default loop count is 1 (or Infinite with duration), not 0.

coding.title: Thread start schedule
coding.prompt:
Write `start_times(threads, ramp_up)` returning a list of start times in seconds (floats) for each thread: thread `i` (0-based) starts at `i * ramp_up / threads`.

Example: `start_times(4, 8)` returns `[0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0]`. With `ramp_up` 0 all threads start at `0.0`.
coding.solution:
def start_times(threads, ramp_up):
    return [i * ramp_up / threads for i in range(threads)]
coding.explanation: JMeter spaces thread starts evenly across ramp-up, which is why the last thread starts just before the ramp-up ends rather than exactly at it.
hints: The gap between starts is `ramp_up / threads`.
`[i * ramp_up / threads for i in range(threads)]`

tests.name: Fractional gap
tests.code:
r = start_times(3, 1)
assert len(r) == 3 and abs(r[2] - 2/3) < 1e-9, r

coding.title: Active users at time t
coding.prompt:
A Thread Group has `threads`, `ramp_up` seconds and a duration of `duration` seconds (threads stop at `duration`). Thread `i` starts at `i * ramp_up / threads`. Write `active_at(threads, ramp_up, duration, t)` returning how many threads are running at time `t` (a thread counts if `start <= t < duration`).

Example: `active_at(20, 60, 30, 29)` returns `10` (threads start every 3 s at 0, 3, ..., 27).
coding.explanation: Counting started threads at time t and zeroing after the duration models how a too-short duration cuts the ramp-up off, the bug in the debugging question above.
hints: Count threads whose start time is `<= t`.
`sum(1 for i in range(threads) if i * ramp_up / threads <= t)`
